| Standard | Scope | Key Requirements for This SDL | Legally Binding in US University? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 | Safety of industrial robots and integrated robot applications; Part 1 addresses robot manufacturers, Part 2 integrators and robot cells. | Perform cell-level risk assessment; define safeguarded, restricted, operational, and collaborative spaces; provide validated protective stops, emergency stops, mode control, access protection, restart prevention, and integration/validation documentation. The complete arm–tool–workpiece–furnace cell must be assessed—not merely the PiPER arm. Collaborative operation does not remove guarding requirements where hot, sharp, reactive, or crushing hazards cannot be acceptably limited. (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **Usually not directly statutory.** A voluntary consensus standard, but it may become the recognized benchmark through contracts, university EHS policy, insurer conditions, an adopted code, or OSHA evidence of feasible hazard control. | The 2025 revision should be checked against the institution’s adopted ANSI/RIA edition. It does not grant blanket permission for unattended operation; suitability follows from the application risk assessment and validated safety functions. Published SDL literature located here does not demonstrate third-party ISO 10218 certification. (pqac-00000070, pqac-00000072) |
| ISO/TS 15066:2016 | Supplemental guidance for collaborative industrial robot applications. | Select and validate one or more collaborative methods: safety-rated monitored stop, hand guiding, speed-and-separation monitoring, or power-and-force limiting. Assess the end effector, payload, fixtures, trapping geometry, transient contact, and quasi-static contact—not just nominal arm force. (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **No, unless incorporated** into policy, contract, approval conditions, or a legally enforceable duty. | It addresses human–robot collaboration, not furnace, combustible-dust, or reactive-material safety. If nobody is present, “collaborative” capability is largely irrelevant; hazardous process and unexpected-entry risks still require safeguarding. |
| ISO 13849-1:2023 | Design of safety-related parts of machinery control systems using Performance Levels, PL a–e. | Derive the required PL for each safety function from risk; design suitable architecture/category, component reliability, diagnostic coverage, common-cause-failure resistance, and systematic controls. Validate separately under ISO 13849-2. Safety functions may include guard-door stopping, restart inhibit, emergency stop, furnace-door permissives, and exhaust/grounding interlocks. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) | **Not independently statutory**, but commonly used to substantiate that safety controls meet the recognized state of practice. | PL is assigned **per safety function**, not to the laboratory as a whole. A PL e-capable relay cannot make an uncertified robot reaction path PL e; end-to-end claims require evidence for sensing, logic, output, and final stopping elements. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| IEC 62061:2021 | Functional safety of safety-related control systems for machinery using SIL 1–3 and SIL claim limits. | Determine required SIL for each safety-related control function; allocate and verify integrity across sensors, logic, communication, and actuators; control random hardware and systematic failures; validate the integrated function. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) | **Not independently statutory** in the United States; an alternative machinery-functional-safety route that EHS, integrators, or insurers may accept. | Do not casually translate PL to SIL or claim SIL 3 because individual components support it. The complete safety function and its interfaces must satisfy the claimed integrity. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003) |
| IEC 61508 series | Generic lifecycle standard for electrical/electronic/programmable-electronic functional safety systems. | Apply a safety lifecycle where machinery-specific standards do not adequately cover a function: hazard analysis, safety requirements allocation, independence, systematic-capability controls, verification, validation, configuration management, proof testing, and change control. | **Normally not directly binding** on a university SDL. It may be invoked contractually or used as the parent framework for a separately engineered safety-instrumented function. | ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061 is ordinarily more directly applicable to machinery. IEC 61508 is not a certification shortcut for Raspberry Pis, MQTT, ordinary PLCs, cameras, or cloud services. (pqac-00000074) |
| ANSI/RIA R15.06 | United States national robot-safety consensus standard, historically harmonized with ISO 10218. | Require application risk assessment, safeguarding, safe operating procedures, training, lockout/tagout coordination, validation, and documentation for the integrated robot system. | **Consensus standard, not automatically federal law.** It can nevertheless establish recognized industry practice and may be imposed by institutional policy, contract, insurer, or authority having jurisdiction. | The institution must confirm which edition it recognizes and how the 2025 ISO revision maps to the current US adoption; do not assume automatic equivalence. (pqac-00000070) |
| OSH Act §5(a)(1) General Duty Clause; 29 CFR 1910.212 machine guarding | Federal worker-safety duty and general machine-guarding requirement. | Protect employees from recognized serious hazards using feasible controls; guard points of operation, nip points, rotating parts, flying material, and similar hazards. Applicable controls can include fixed/interlocked barriers, presence sensing, lockout/tagout, training, and documented safe work practices. | **Yes for covered employees and workplaces.** Coverage of students who are not employees varies, but employed students, staff, and faculty workers are generally covered; state-plan rules may differ. | **Correction:** 29 CFR 1910.212 is not the General Duty Clause; the General Duty Clause is OSH Act §5(a)(1). Consensus standards may be evidence of hazard recognition and feasible abatement, but they do not become federal regulations merely by being cited. |
| NFPA 484, *Standard for Combustible Metals*; current successor/adopted-edition check required | Fire and explosion prevention for combustible metals, including powder handling, dust collection, housekeeping, ignition control, bonding/grounding, and metal-fire response. | Obtain material-specific explosibility data; minimize dust release and accumulation; control ignition and static; bond and ground conductive equipment; evaluate electrical-area classification; use compatible dedicated collection/exhaust; prevent incompatible-metal or water contact; provide appropriate Class D agents and emergency procedures. | **Binding only if adopted** by state/local code, incorporated by the authority having jurisdiction, university policy, insurer condition, or contract. Many jurisdictions enforce an adopted NFPA edition by reference. | NFPA consolidated combustible-dust standards into **NFPA 660** beginning with the 2025 edition; determine whether the local authority still enforces NFPA 484 or has adopted NFPA 660. Material behavior varies strongly with particle size and process conditions, so generic values are not a design basis. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| ISO 12100:2010 | Machinery risk-assessment and risk-reduction methodology. | Define limits and intended/reasonably foreseeable misuse; identify hazards over the full lifecycle; estimate and evaluate risk; reduce risk in order through inherently safe design, engineering safeguards, then information/training; document residual risk and iterate after modifications. | **Voluntary consensus standard**, unless incorporated into an enforceable requirement or institutional approval. | Best baseline for the machinery risk-assessment file, supplemented here by process HAZOP for furnace/powder nodes, FMEA/FMECA for component faults, and STPA for orchestration, remote supervision, software, and unsafe control interactions. STPA is particularly useful where hazards arise without a component failure. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) |


*Table: This table separates statutory duties from voluntary consensus standards and identifies what each framework contributes to a US university SDL. It also corrects the common conflation of OSHA’s General Duty Clause with 29 CFR 1910.212 and flags NFPA 660’s consolidation of NFPA 484.*
